A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same graph-theoretic study, with readable main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices. The experimental restructuring can be matched, including v2 result plots retained in v4 Appendix L.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix K report original experiments measuring retrieval accuracy, positional preferences, and attention sinks in trained attention networks.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices K–L report original retrieval and attention-sink results, including additional depth, residual-connection, and input-geometry experiments.

M1.justification: The proposed analytical framework, attention update in Equation 1, masks, and positional encodings are unchanged. Residual and pure-attention variants are distinguished as experimental configurations; v2 Figure 2 is retained as v4 Figure 14 and explicitly identified as using residual connections.

E1.justification: v4 provides distinct result sets for Gaussian-mixture inputs and fixed-vocabulary, anisotropic embeddings, plus a preliminary isotropic condition with lambda = 0. This broadens the tested input conditions within the same synthetic retrieval task. The original v2 plots survive under the fixed-vocabulary description in Appendix L, so that appendix is not entirely new coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain No PE, decay mask, and RoPE for depth experiments, and No PE, sinusoidal PE, and RoPE under complete versus causal masking for training-bias experiments. Attention-sink comparisons retain causal, sliding-window, and prefix masks. Residual controls and depth configurations change the experimental design, rather than adding an external comparison method.

E3.justification: v4 adds explicit residual/no-residual controls and pure-attention depth sweeps at 2, 4, and 6 layers, alongside residual sweeps at 2, 6, and 10 layers. Retrieval metrics, 10,000-sequence test sets, and training budgets remain unchanged. Appendix J also changes the written sampling normalization, without establishing whether the implementation changed.

E4.justification: Section 5.1 and Appendices K.1–K.2 add a substantive investigation of how residual connections interact with depth and positional encoding, exposing departures from the earlier simple depth-amplification pattern. Appendix L adds a pure-attention fixed-vocabulary sweep and a preliminary anisotropy check, testing whether embedding geometry affects these behaviors.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-run averages for Figures 2 and 3. v4 introduces no documented change to run counts, seed reporting, uncertainty estimation, confidence intervals, or significance testing.

E6.justification: All v2 result plots are retained in Appendix L, while v4 adds Gaussian-mixture counterparts and additional architecture/depth results. For example, v4 Figure 5 reports No PE residual-model first-versus-last gaps of 0.266, 0.138, and 0.015 at depths 2, 6, and 10, revealing decreasing bias. These are setting-specific additions, not demonstrated performance gains over the retained v2 results.

T1.justification: The analytical definitions, assumptions A1–A3, theorem and lemma statements, derivations, and proofs in Sections 3–4 and Appendices A–I are unchanged. The revised sampling descriptions concern experimental settings.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same contributions: a graph-theoretic framework, early-token bias from causal masking, and competition between masking and relative positional encodings. The conclusion preserves these central claims; added qualifications appear in the experimental interpretation.

C2.justification: v4 qualifies the earlier depth-amplification interpretation by showing that residual connections can amplify or reduce bias depending on depth and positional encoding. It also acknowledges lost-in-the-middle behavior in deep RoPE models without biased training data, qualifying v2's data-bias explanation. Appendix L introduces embedding geometry and task difficulty as possible explanations for differences between input regimes.

D1.justification: v4 documents residual placement and the fixed-vocabulary generator, including its shared Gaussian component and anisotropy parameter lambda = 0.75. Code access, hardware, optimizer, and training-budget disclosures are retained. Appendix J introduces epsilon in the noise formula but still specifies gamma = 0.75, leaving a reproducibility ambiguity.

R1.justification: Appendix L adds five references concerning embedding geometry and anisotropy: Ait-Saada and Nadif, Cai et al., Ethayarajh, Gao et al., and Godey et al. These motivate the fixed-vocabulary setting; Section 2 and the paper's central positioning relative to prior work remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The prose changes are localized: Section 5 gains residual and geometry explanations, Appendix K gains two subsections, its existing discussions move to K.3–K.4, and Appendix L separates the fixed-vocabulary material. The abstract, introduction, related-work narrative, and theoretical exposition remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: The experimental displays are substantially expanded and reorganized. Figure 2 gains residual/depth groupings and a revised legend, additional plots populate Appendix K, and v2 Figures 2–10 move to v4 Figures 14–18 and 20–23. Appendix L also groups retained plots under collective captions. Figure 1 and Table 1 remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 provides better controlled and more qualified empirical support by separating residual from pure-attention behavior and distinguishing input regimes. The deep-RoPE exception also improves the earlier interpretation of lost-in-the-middle behavior. These gains support a modest overall improvement, although Appendix J's unresolved epsilon/gamma inconsistency limits reproducibility and the new geometry explanation remains preliminary.
